column2: The Woman Talking Straight To Camera
column3: Wants a peer's unedited verdict with no set and no script; the plainness is the proof.
Has cycled through products and given up; almost gave up meets her at the point of resignation rather than of hope.
Needs a physical stunt before she will believe a claim; pouring water over finished hair is a test she could not run herself.
Exhausted by multi-step routines; transforming frizz with a single bottle is a promise about her time, not her hair.
Wants to test an expensive product at low cost and low commitment; the small format is the entry point.
Chasing one very specific finish that has a name online; the reference look is the specification.
Being addressed by an unusually specific hair description; the precision is what convinces her it was made for her type.
Films her own routine and needs products that survive being shown; the towel and the tool are the context.
Wants the full set recommended together rather than one hero; the dream team framing removes the decision of what to pair.
Judges everything on the final mirror shot; the length and shine at the end is the only argument she needs.
Has invested in unnatural colour and now needs products that will not strip it; the colour in frame is the qualification.
Scans for hair that looks like hers before listening; the model's curl pattern is the filter.
Buys sets to line up on a shelf; the tray presentation is aspiration for her own bathroom.
Buys where she already has points and returns; the retailer is the reassurance, the product is the choice.
Reached by something that does not look like advertising; a tear-off flyer in a city buys curiosity a feed ad cannot.
Wants the product summarised without a story; five words is a promise to waste none of her time.
Owns the products and does not know the sequence; answering the order question is a service that sells the set.
Trusts a slow, casual account of an ongoing habit over any before-and-after.
Defers to a masthead's pick; the CNN attribution is doing the whole job.
Buying an unstyled look that in fact requires product; the relaxed pose is the deliverable.
Has bought the bottle and is now buying against waste and price; the refill signals commitment to the brand.
Wants to see professional hands work; smooth, sculpt, shine is a sequence of actions rather than benefits.
Buying an object that will read as expensive without shouting; the muted bottle on a blank ground is the point.
Needs lift without weight and is watching for how the spray falls; texture is a physics problem to her.
Treats a three-thousand-person waitlist as proof of efficacy; back in stock is the trigger to buy immediately.
Extending time between washes; the clip and the smoothed root are what she is actually buying.
Has paid for colour and now buys defensively; a matched shampoo and conditioner pair is insurance on that spend.
Has a specific styling problem created by a specific haircut; naming bangs in summer is precise enough to feel personal.
Has been let down by volume products that collapse by lunch; day-one persistence is the claim being tested.
Wants a person holding the bottle and saying what it does; the demonstration is the format she trusts.
Buying an unusual format and needs to understand why it exists; the reason is the hook, the product is second.
Buys the whole picture; the styling and the light are the product and the bottles are props.
Trusts humour and low production as evidence nobody is performing at her.

column2: The Category Sceptic Holding The Bottle
column3: Being asked to accept an unfamiliar product type; the hand-held demo is what makes a shampoo-replacement legible.
Blocked entirely by the fear that her hair type is the exception; try it for zero dollars is aimed at that objection alone.
Believes conventional shampoo has been damaging her; the reframing is the sale.
A professional buyer being sold on margin, not efficacy; the earnings quote is the pitch.
Understands the beauty grammar being borrowed; naming the look tells her exactly what finish to expect.
Buys tins with heritage branding; the tin itself signals a barbershop lineage the formula never claims.
Buying membership in a grooming tradition; the shop, the tattoos and the supply-co framing are the product.
